skills.name: Giant covalent structures: diamond and graphite

note.text:
Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon (allotropes) but have different structures.
• Diamond: each carbon is covalently bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3-D tetrahedral network. Very hard, very high m.p., does not conduct (no free electrons). Uses: cutting and drilling tools, jewellery.
• Graphite: each carbon bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers; the fourth electron is delocalised. Layers are held by weak forces and slide over each other. Soft and slippery, conducts electricity, high m.p. Uses: pencil 'lead', lubricant, electrodes.

sections.heading: Same element, two structures
sections.text:
Diamond and graphite are both made only of carbon atoms. Different forms of the same element are called allotropes.
Their properties are very different because their atoms are joined in different ways. Both are giant covalent structures: no small molecules, just huge networks of bonded atoms.

sections.heading: Diamond
sections.text:
Each carbon atom forms {4} covalent bonds to four other carbon atoms, arranged as a tetrahedron. This makes a rigid three-dimensional network.
• Extremely hard: used on drill tips and cutting tools.
• Very high melting point.
• Does not conduct: all outer electrons are in bonds.
• Sparkles when cut: used in jewellery.

sections.heading: Graphite
sections.text:
Each carbon atom bonds to only {3} others, forming flat layers of hexagons. The fourth outer electron of each atom is delocalised, free to move along the layer.
• Layers held by weak forces slide easily: soft and slippery, used in pencils and as a lubricant.
• Conducts electricity: used for electrodes and in batteries.
• High melting point, like diamond.

key_words.meaning: different forms of the same element
a huge network of atoms joined by covalent bonds
an electron free to move, not tied to one bond

mistake.wrong: Graphite is soft because its covalent bonds are weak
mistake.right: Graphite is soft because the forces between its layers are weak
mistake.why: The bonds within each layer are strong; it is the layers that slide.

worked_example.problem: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.
steps: In diamond, all four outer electrons of each carbon are used in covalent bonds: none are free.
In graphite, each carbon uses only {3} electrons in bonds; the {4}th is delocalised along the layers.
These free electrons carry the current.
worked_example.answer: Graphite has one free electron per carbon atom; diamond has none

cards.idea: Diamond: each carbon bonded to {4} others in a rigid network.
Graphite: layers of carbon (each bonded to {3}) that slide over each other.
example: Pencil marks are layers of graphite left on paper.

cards.idea: Graphite conducts because each carbon has {1} free electron.
example: Graphite electrodes are used in electrolysis.

pick.q: Both diamond and graphite have very high melting points. Why?
pick.r: Both are giant structures with many strong covalent bonds to break
w: Both are made of small molecules
pick.y: Melting means breaking strong covalent bonds throughout.

pick.q: Pencil 'lead' leaves a mark on paper. Why?
pick.r: Layers of graphite slide off onto the paper
e: Pencils contain graphite, not lead metal.
Graphite does not melt at room temperature.
pick.y: Weak forces between layers let them flake off.

pick.y: Conduction needs free electrons; diamond has none.
